_README: GENERATED by tools/build_builds.mjs from tools/builds-curated.json plus app/data/<group>.json.
Never hand-edit: the next refresh overwrites it. Edit builds-curated.json and re-run the generator.
It carries NO game numbers on purpose - every level, tier and stat the Builds tab prints is read at
runtime from the same entity record the Items tab reads, so the two screens cannot disagree.
validate.mjs group X fails the build if a number ever appears in here.
ruling: These are hand-picked starter builds, not a ranking. Path of Exile 2 publishes no match-outcome data, so nothing here is scored against wins and no build is claimed to be better than another. Every pick names the real gem or item it points at, and the reason under it is why that pick is in this list - not a promise that nothing else would work.

builds.name: Warrior slam opener
builds.forWho: For a first character who wants to walk in, hit things hard and survive being hit back.

beginner.whatItIs: A melee build around the slam the Warrior starts the game holding, with supports that make the slam land wider and stagger what it hits, and gear that keeps your life and armour climbing while you learn the fights.
beginner.whyItMatters: It asks almost nothing of you in the first act. The skill is already in your hands, the supports drop early, and the gear pieces are ones you can pick up or trade for without planning a whole passive tree first. That leaves your attention on dodging and positioning, which is what actually kills you early.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Start here if this is your first character in Path of Exile 2 and you would rather learn the fights than learn a build. Move on from it once you have a weapon you like better than the one listed and a clear idea of the damage type you want to scale.

picks.why: The Warrior begins holding this one, so the build works from your first minute of play with nothing to find first. It is a slam with an area of effect, which means one button answers both a single enemy and a pack.
It supports melee attacks and makes them build heavy stun faster. Staggering a dangerous enemy buys you the half second you need to reposition, which matters more early than raw damage does.

It grants rage when your melee attack hits, so the longer a fight runs the harder you swing. Slow, heavy skills like this one are the ones that benefit from a resource that builds while you commit to a swing.
It makes an area skill cover more ground. A slam that reaches the second row of a pack clears at a completely different speed to one that only reaches the first.

A travel skill that is also an attack, so you close distance and open the fight with the same button. Having any movement skill on your bar is the difference between escaping a bad pull and dying in it.

The Warrior starts with a tower shield, and this is the skill that puts it between you and the hit. Learning to raise it before a telegraphed attack is the single habit that carries a melee character through the campaign.

A one-handed mace that adds flat physical damage, accuracy and strength at once. Early on, flat damage added to a slow weapon is worth far more than a percentage increase, and the strength helps you meet requirements on the rest of your gear.

A shield with a large armour increase, strength, and life regeneration that ticks whether or not you are in a fight. Regeneration is the defensive stat that keeps working while you walk between packs, so it saves flask charges for the moments that actually need them.
The piece to aim for rather than start with: armour, maximum life and life regeneration on one slot. It is the level requirement that sets when this whole build is fully assembled.

It turns a plain item into a magic one with a modifier. Spending one on a white weapon or shield that has fallen behind is usually worth more than hoarding it, because the unique pieces above can take a long time to appear.

builds.name: Huntress spear opener
builds.forWho: For someone who wants to be in melee range but moving constantly rather than standing and trading.

beginner.whatItIs: A spear build around the spinning strike the Huntress starts with, supported for attack speed and reach, wearing evasion gear and boots that keep you fast.
beginner.whyItMatters: The Huntress does not want to stand still. Everything here pushes in the same direction: hit more often, hit a wider circle, and be somewhere else before the counterattack lands. Her gear gives evasion rather than armour, which means she avoids hits instead of absorbing them, so the defensive stats a Warrior wants do very little on her.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Pick this up on your first Huntress, or when a ranged character has left you wanting something with more contact. Drop it once you have found a spear you would rather scale than the one listed.

picks.why: The Huntress starts holding it. It is a melee strike with an area of effect, so it answers a single target and a surrounding pack with the same input, which suits a character who is always mid-movement.
It supports attacks and makes them faster. On a skill you spend the whole fight repeating, attack speed is felt on every single swing rather than only on the big ones.
It supports melee strike skills and adds an aftershock that damages the area around the hit. That turns a strike aimed at one enemy into something that also touches the ones behind it.
It widens an area skill. On a spin attack, extra radius is extra targets per swing, so it does more for your clear speed than a damage increase of the same size would.
A travel skill that works no matter what weapon you are holding, so it stays useful through every rebuild. Keep it bound from level one and use it to leave, not to arrive.
A spear with added physical damage and extra melee strike range. Reach is a defensive stat on a melee character, because a hit you land from further out is a hit you take fewer counterattacks for.
Evasion, dexterity and movement speed while you are on full life. It rewards exactly the playstyle this build wants: stay untouched, stay moving.
Movement speed, maximum life and stun threshold on one slot. The level requirement here is what sets when the build is fully assembled.
It adds a second modifier to a magic item. Save these for a magic spear or a pair of magic boots that already rolled something you want, rather than spending them on the first white item you see.

builds.name: Mercenary crossbow opener
builds.forWho: For someone who wants to fight at range and reload rather than dodge in and out of melee.

beginner.whatItIs: A crossbow build around the ammunition skill the Mercenary starts with, supported to load more bolts and land more of them, with a crossbow and a helmet that patch the two things a ranged character runs short of early.
beginner.whyItMatters: Crossbow skills in Path of Exile 2 work on loaded ammunition rather than a plain attack loop, so the supports that matter are the ones that change how much you load and how fast you fire it. Projectile supports that would help a bow do much less here, because the limit on your damage is the magazine rather than the arrow.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Use this for a first Mercenary or a first ranged character. Move off it once you have a crossbow with modifiers you want to keep and a clear damage type to scale.

picks.why: The Mercenary begins with it loaded. It is an ammunition skill with an area of effect, so one magazine handles a group, which is what a ranged character struggles with before any gear arrives.

It supports crossbow ammunition skills and loads an extra bolt, at the cost of reload speed. More shots per magazine is what actually raises your damage on a skill measured in bolts rather than in swings.
It supports attacks and makes them faster, which on a crossbow means you empty a loaded magazine sooner and spend more of the fight shooting.
It grants accuracy to attacks. A missed shot on a limited magazine costs you a reload as well as the damage, so accuracy is worth more here than it looks on paper.
A travel skill that does not care which weapon you hold. A ranged character's whole defence is the gap between them and the enemy, and this is how you re-open it.
A crossbow with added cold damage, mana returned on kill, and increased freeze buildup. Freezing what you shoot is a defensive layer as well as damage, since a frozen enemy is not walking at you.

A helmet that grants a large block of elemental resistance plus evasion and item rarity. Resistance is the stat the campaign quietly punishes you for ignoring, and this covers all three at once. Its level requirement sets when the build is fully assembled.

It upgrades a plain or magic item straight to a rare with four random modifiers. Used on a crossbow base at your level it gives you four modifiers in one step, which is why it is worth holding for a weapon slot rather than spending on armour.

builds.name: Monk quarterstaff opener
builds.forWho: For someone who likes fast melee and does not mind aiming a skill rather than swinging at what is in front of them.

beginner.whatItIs: A quarterstaff build around the lightning slam the Monk starts with, supported for speed, reach and lightning damage, with a staff that adds flat damage and boots that keep you moving.
beginner.whyItMatters: The Monk's opening skill is both a melee slam and a projectile, so it covers the range gap that usually kills fast melee characters early. Everything else here is chosen to keep that one button good instead of spreading you across three skills you cannot fund.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Take this on a first Monk. Leave it behind when you have decided whether you want to scale the lightning damage or the physical damage, because that choice changes the supports.

picks.why: The Monk starts holding it. It is a slam that also sends out a projectile, so the same button hits the enemy in your face and the one across the room.
It supports attacks and makes them faster. The Monk's damage comes from repetition rather than from one heavy hit, so speed is the stat the build is actually built on.
It adds lightning damage while reducing cold and fire damage. That trade costs this skill almost nothing, because its damage is already lightning rather than the two types being reduced.
It widens an area skill. On a slam you are aiming into a pack, extra radius means fewer enemies survive to reach you.
A melee strike to keep on the bar for single enemies that do not need an area skill spent on them. Having a cheap second attack stops you burning resources on a slam aimed at one target.

A quarterstaff with added physical damage, strength, and bleeding on hit. Flat added damage on a fast weapon is felt on every hit, and the bleed keeps damaging a target after you have moved on to the next one.

Boots with a large movement speed increase plus energy shield and dexterity. Movement speed helps you reach a fight, leave one, and cross a zone, so it keeps paying on a character built around repetition. Its level requirement sets when this build is fully assembled.
It turns a plain item into a magic one with a modifier. On a fast character, upgrading a white quarterstaff or a white pair of gloves keeps your damage moving between real drops.

builds.name: Ranger bow opener
builds.forWho: For someone who wants to clear whole screens from a distance and never be touched.

beginner.whatItIs: A bow build around the lightning arrow the Ranger starts with, supported to fire more arrows that chain between enemies, with a quiver and a helmet that cover damage and resistance.
beginner.whyItMatters: The Ranger's opening skill already chains between enemies, so supports that add projectiles and chains multiply something the skill does rather than bolting on something new. That is why this build works from the first act rather than only after a lot of investment.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Use it for a first Ranger or any first bow character. Reconsider it once you have a bow worth scaling and know whether you are staying on lightning damage.

picks.why: The Ranger begins with it. It fires a projectile that chains to further enemies and deals lightning damage in an area, which means it clears a group from one shot without you moving.
It supports projectile skills and adds extra projectiles, at some cost to attack and cast speed. Each added arrow is another chain start, so it compounds with what this skill already does.
It makes a chaining skill chain more times. This skill already chains, so the support extends an effect that is doing the clearing rather than adding a second thing to think about.
It makes a hit more likely to shock. A shocked enemy takes more damage from everything that hits it afterwards, and your arrows are already lightning, so no conversion is needed.
A bow skill that moves you and leaves damage behind you. On a character with very little armour, the skill that gets you out of a bad position is a defensive item, not a utility one.
A quiver with added cold damage to attacks, attack speed and cold resistance. The quiver slot does nothing for you until you fill it, and this one covers offence and one resistance at the same time.
A bow whose whole point is that it multiplies the bonuses your quiver gives. It pairs with the quiver above, which is why the two are listed together rather than separately.

Elemental resistance across all three types plus evasion and rarity. A character who dies to a single spell is usually a character with unfilled resistances, and this fills them in one slot. Its level requirement sets when the build is fully assembled.
It adds a modifier to a magic item. Hold these for a magic quiver or magic bow that already rolled added damage, rather than spending them on the first upgrade you find.

builds.name: Sorceress lightning opener
builds.forWho: For someone who wants to fill a room with damage and watch it die, and who is willing to manage mana.

beginner.whatItIs: A spell build around the lightning projectiles the Sorceress starts with, supported for raw spell damage and mana sustain, with a staff that raises spell damage and a ring that removes a way to be locked down.
beginner.whyItMatters: A caster's early problem is usually mana rather than damage. One of the three supports here and both of the items are picked for mana instead of damage, because a spell build that runs dry mid-fight deals nothing at all no matter what the numbers on the staff say.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Take this on a first Sorceress. Move off it when you have found a staff worth building around or decided to commit to one element instead of the two this skill deals.

picks.why: The Sorceress begins with it. It fires projectiles that persist and bounce, so in a closed room a single cast keeps dealing damage after you have started moving.
It supports spells that hit and raises their damage, in exchange for giving up critical hits. Early on you have almost no critical hit chance to give up, so the trade costs you very little.
It tracks the mana you spend and rewards you once you have spent enough. It answers the caster's real early problem, which is running out of mana rather than running out of damage.
It makes hits more likely to shock, and a shocked enemy takes more damage from what lands next. This skill already deals lightning damage, so nothing has to be converted first.
A stationary lightning area you drop and leave. Cast it on a boss and it keeps working while you spend your attention on dodging, which is where a caster's attention should be.
A staff with a large spell damage increase, cast speed and mana regeneration. The mana regeneration is the part that makes it a starter item rather than only a damage item.

A ring with maximum mana, mana regeneration, and outright immunity to being chilled or frozen. Being frozen as a caster usually means dying, so this removes a whole category of death. Its level requirement sets when the build is fully assembled.
It improves the quality of a wand, staff or sceptre. Quality on a caster weapon raises the spell damage it already gives, so these are worth saving for the staff you intend to keep.

builds.name: Witch minion opener
builds.forWho: For someone who would rather command a fight than stand in one.

beginner.whatItIs: A minion build around raised skeletons, supported to keep them alive and resistant, with the Witch's own starting spell used to make the corpses they are raised from, plus a sceptre and a focus that make minions tougher.
beginner.whyItMatters: Minions take the hits you would otherwise take, which makes this the gentlest way to learn boss patterns. The trade is that your damage is only as good as your minions' survival, so three of the supports here buy survival rather than damage on purpose.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Start here if dying to things you did not see coming is what stops you finishing a campaign. Move on once you understand which minion type you want to scale, because the supports differ for each.

picks.why: A persistent minion that stays raised rather than expiring on a timer, so your army is standing when the next fight starts instead of needing to be rebuilt.

It makes minions take less damage and deal less. On a build whose damage only happens while the minions are alive, trading some of their damage for their survival usually gives you more damage overall.
It raises minions' elemental resistances. Campaign bosses kill minions with elemental damage far more often than with physical, which is what makes this the resistance worth buying first.
It lets a persistent minion keep fighting after a hit that would have killed it. That converts the moment your army evaporates into a few extra seconds of damage.

The Witch starts with this one, and it creates corpses. A minion build without a corpse source stalls the moment a room is cleared, so this stays on the bar even after other spells replace it as damage.
A sceptre with maximum mana, intelligence and mana regeneration. The sceptre is the Witch's minion weapon and she begins with one, so this is a same-slot upgrade rather than a rebuild.

A focus that raises minion maximum life, plus energy shield and mana regeneration for you. It buys the same thing the supports do, which is minions that are still standing. Its level requirement sets when the build is fully assembled.
It turns a plain item into a magic one with a modifier. Minion modifiers appear on sceptres and on the off-hand, so upgrading white items in those two slots is where these are worth spending.

builds.name: Druid fire opener
builds.forWho: For someone happy to hold a button down and control ground rather than chase enemies around.

beginner.whatItIs: A spell build around the burning eruption the Druid starts with, supported for spell damage, area and ignite chance, with a staff that adds fire damage to everything you cast and body armour that covers life and fire resistance.
beginner.whyItMatters: This skill damages whatever stands in the area it creates, so its value is decided by how much ground it covers and how long things stay in it. That is why the supports here buy area and burning rather than raw hit damage.
beginner.whenToUseIt: Take it on a first Druid, especially if you want to learn the class before touching its animal forms. Move on once you have decided whether you are scaling the fire damage or the shapeshifting side of the class.

picks.why: The Druid begins holding it. It raises a burning eruption that keeps damaging whatever stands on it, so one cast covers ground instead of hitting once and ending.
It raises the damage of a spell that hits, in exchange for giving up critical hits. A new character has very little critical hit chance to lose, so the exchange is close to free.
It makes an area skill larger. On a skill whose damage is decided by how much ground it covers, area is the same thing as damage.
It makes a hit more likely to ignite. An ignited enemy keeps burning after it leaves your eruption, which patches the gap this skill has against anything that walks out of the area.
A travel skill that works with any weapon. A character who plants an area and stands near it needs one reliable way to not be standing there when something arrives.

A staff that converts part of your damage into extra fire damage, raises spell damage, and returns life on kill. It suits a fire build on both counts, and the life on kill covers a class that carries no shield.
Body armour with maximum life, strength, and a large block of fire resistance. Its level requirement sets when this build is fully assembled.
It adds a modifier to a magic item. Save them for a magic staff or magic body armour that already rolled something worth keeping, rather than spending on a first upgrade.
